- Mostly coding
- Annoying bits, like Jira
- Scripting and Tools: VSCode, Git, etc
- Cut and paste GPT?

## The 3-5x developer

- Planning with AI help
- Coding is mostly Cursor, Codex, or Claude
    - From the most to least expensive task
- You might have an `AGENTS.md`
- Tried a skill or two: `/superpowers`, `/grill-me`, etc.
- Used `/review` or CodeRabbit, GitHub, Copilot
- Most corporate devs are here right now

## `AGENTS.md` Makes Context Persistent

- Explains how this repository actually works
- Names the build, test, and review commands
- Records boundaries, conventions, and the definition of done
- Gives every agent the same starting point
- Turns repeated corrections into permanent guidance
- Changes with the code—and can be reviewed with it

<p class="big-idea">Stop re-prompting the rules.<br><span class="accent">Version them.</span></p>

## The 3-5x Trap

<p class="big-idea">The code got faster.<br><span class="accent-orange">The rest of the job did not.</span></p>

<div class="card-grid three">
  <div class="idea-card orange"><strong>Manual hand-offs</strong>You copy plans, results, and context between tools.</div>
  <div class="idea-card orange"><strong>Manual checking</strong>You inspect every result because the workflow cannot prove it worked.</div>
  <div class="idea-card orange"><strong>You are the glue</strong>The AI stops whenever you stop pushing it.</div>
</div>

## The Jump to 10x

<div class="card-grid three">
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>3–5x</strong>AI helps with individual tasks.<br><br><span class="dim">You drive.</span></div>
  <div class="idea-card orange"><strong>10x</strong>Automation moves small slices through the whole loop.<br><br><span class="dim">You check the steps.</span></div>
  <div class="idea-card red"><strong>100x</strong>The system handles routine checking too.<br><br><span class="dim">You watch outcomes.</span></div>
</div>

<p class="plain-note">The practical jump is from the first box to the second.</p>

## Every Box Becomes a Skill

<div class="pipeline">
  <span class="step">Jira</span><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Planning</span><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Coding</span><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Testing</span>
</div>

<div class="pipeline">
  <span class="step">Review</span><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Commit</span><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Deploy</span><span class="arrow">→</span>
  <span class="step">Docs</span>
</div>

<p class="plain-note">Each skill owns one capability, its tools, and its checks. The orchestrator carries evidence to the next step.</p>

<p class="big-idea"><span class="accent">Automate every step.</span><br>Skills make the automation reusable.</p>

## Skills: The Basic Structure

```text
my-skill/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   └── do_the_work.py
├── references/
└── assets/
```

<p class="plain-note"><code>SKILL.md</code> explains when to use the skill. The supporting files make the work repeatable.</p>

## Skills: Keep Them Thin

- A little Markdown defines the trigger, inputs, and boundaries
- Small Python tools do the repeatable work
- Each tool is easy to run, test, and repair
- An orchestrator skill selects and sequences the thin skills
- Failures stay local instead of derailing the whole workflow

<p class="big-idea"><span class="accent">Markdown routes.</span> Python works.<br>The orchestrator conducts.</p>

## Skills save Tokens

![](screenshots/token-cost.png){.slide-image fig-alt="Token usage and cost showing approximately 286 million tokens and 191 dollars"}

## The Whole Loop Becomes a Skill Tree

```text
project/
├── plans/
│   └── manifesto.md
└── .agents/
    └── skills/
        └── orchestrator.md
            ├── jira/
            ├── coding/
            ├── slack/
            ├── perforce/       # source control
            ├── swarm/          # reviews
            └── preflight/
```

<p class="plain-note"><code>orchestrator.md</code> chooses the workflow and delegates each step to a child skill.</p>

## A Preflight Skill Clears the Runway

- Start the MCPs and local services the workflow needs
- Check credentials, ports, and required configuration
- Probe every dependency before real work begins
- Report what is ready, degraded, or blocked
- Stop early when the environment cannot support the run

<p class="big-idea">No agent starts work<br><span class="accent-orange">until the runway is clear.</span></p>

## The Orchestrator Selects the Workflow

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}

```text
workflows/
├── automated-reviewer.md
├── bug-feature-implementation.md
├── submit-workflow.md
└── coder.md
```

:::

::: {.column width="58%"}

- **Automated reviewer** checks behavior and evidence
- **Bug/feature implementation** moves one slice through the loop
- **Submit workflow** commits, pushes, and watches the checks
- **Coder** handles a focused implementation step

:::

::::

<p class="big-idea"><span class="accent">The orchestrator chooses the path.</span><br>Thin skills execute the steps.</p>

## `plans/` Gives Intent a Home

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}

```text
plans/
├── manifesto.md
├── feature-plan.md
├── architecture.md
└── decisions.md
```

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

- Plans are Markdown: easy to read, diff, and update
- Each captures intent, slices, constraints, and checks
- Other documents keep decisions close to the work
- `manifesto.md` holds the soul of what you are building

:::

::::

<p class="big-idea">Plans explain the next move.<br><span class="accent-orange">The manifesto protects the direction.</span></p>

## The 10x Developer

- Automation is spread across the whole loop
- Work moves as small, complete slices
- Every step leaves something you can inspect
- You still read code and check between steps
- A failure stops the workflow before it grows
- Every correction improves the next run

## Small Slices, Frequent Checks

<div class="checkpoint-strip">
  <div class="checkpoint"><strong>Plan</strong>One visible outcome<span class="check">✓ Check intent</span></div>
  <div class="checkpoint"><strong>Build</strong>One small diff<span class="check">✓ Read the code</span></div>
  <div class="checkpoint"><strong>Prove</strong>Tests and evidence<span class="check">✓ Check behavior</span></div>
  <div class="checkpoint"><strong>Ship</strong>A safe deployment<span class="check">✓ Check reality</span></div>
</div>

<p class="plain-note">Small enough to understand. Complete enough to matter.</p>

## The Agent Needs Eyes

<div class="card-grid four">
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>Logs</strong>What happened?</div>
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>Screenshots</strong>What changed?</div>
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>Tests</strong>Does it still work?</div>
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>Preview</strong>Does it work for real?</div>
</div>

<p class="big-idea">If the agent cannot see the result,<br><span class="accent-orange">you have to check it manually.</span></p>

## The 10x Playbook {.section-divider}

<p class="big-idea">Make the work <span class="accent">visible</span>,<br>the steps <span class="accent-orange">small</span>,<br>and the result <span class="accent">provable</span>.</p>

## Prompts Don't Compound

- A prompt buys one answer
- A test prevents the same failure forever
- A script makes the result repeatable
- A skill makes the workflow reusable

<p class="big-idea"><span class="accent-orange">Chat history is not infrastructure.</span></p>

## Debug Dumps

- One command captures errors, logs, settings, and state
- The agent reads the dump instead of asking you twenty questions
- Fix, rerun, compare

<p class="big-idea">Ask the program.<br><span class="accent">Not the tired human.</span></p>

## Image Grabs

- Capture the screen at known points
- Attach the image to the task automatically
- Let the agent inspect the real result

<p class="plain-note">“It looks wrong” becomes evidence instead of a conversation.</p>

## Image Diffs

- Keep a trusted “before”
- Render the new version
- Highlight only the changed pixels
- Stop if something unexpected moved

<p class="big-idea"><span class="accent">Show the difference.</span> Skip the guessing.</p>

## Audio Comparisons

- Render the reference and the new output
- Compare volume, timing, silence, and shape
- Make failures visible as a waveform

<p class="big-idea">Some bugs have to be <span class="accent-orange">heard.</span></p>

## Client/Server Round Trip

- Start the real client and server
- Send a real request
- Capture both sides of the conversation
- Fail if either side disagrees

<p class="plain-note">A unit test can pass while the product is still broken.</p>

## Lean Correctness Specs

- Use Lean to specify the correctness of the result.

## Iterative Goals

- Give the agent one clear finish line
- Let it work, test, and correct itself
- Keep the goal alive across many steps
- Stop only on evidence—or a real blocker

## Vertical Slices

- One small behavior, end to end
- UI, logic, test, and deployment together
- Useful enough to try
- Small enough to understand and revert

<p class="big-idea">Do not build three layers.<br><span class="accent">Build one working thing.</span></p>

## Incremental Steps for the Human

- Each step leaves a readable diff
- Each step leaves test evidence
- Each step leaves a short summary
- You can interrupt without losing the plot

## Quick Prototypes

- Ugly but runnable beats perfect but imaginary
- Test the risky idea first
- Throw it away without regret

<p class="plain-note">The prototype answers a question. It is not a promise.</p>

## Quick Deployments

- Give every slice a temporary home
- Run the smoke test there
- Share the real thing, not a screenshot of localhost
- Make rollback boring

## Consistent tooling

- The same command works for you, CI, and the agent
- Setup is written down and repeatable
- No hidden IDE magic
- No wiki scavenger hunt

## Small attack surfaces

- Give the agent the smallest useful task
- Limit files, tools, permissions, and scope
- Prefer reversible changes
- Fewer ways to be wrong means faster trust

## Insane build speeds

- Slow feedback creates large, risky guesses
- Fast feedback lets the agent correct itself
- Seconds invite experiments
- Minutes invite waiting

<p class="big-idea">Build speed is not comfort.<br><span class="accent">It is control.</span></p>

## Everything Markdown

- Plans
- Goals
- Decisions
- Handoffs
- Evidence

<p class="plain-note">Readable by people. Readable by agents. Easy to diff.</p>

## Presentation Fun

## Code Inspection

- Ask for a map, not a guided tour
- Find entry points, data flow, rules, and sharp edges
- Write the map down
- Review the map before changing the code

## 75/25 Rule

- 25%: solve today's problem
- 75%: remove the friction that made it hard
- Add the missing test
- Improve the tool
- Capture the instruction

<p class="big-idea">Ship the fix.<br><span class="accent">Then improve the factory.</span></p>

## Dog Food

- Use the workflow on real work
- Notice every manual rescue
- Put that friction into the backlog
- Run it again until the rescue disappears

## Scriptify

- If you explain it twice, make it a command
- Clear inputs
- Clear output
- Useful exit codes
- Safe to rerun

<p class="big-idea">A script is a tiny tool<br>that never forgets the steps.</p>

## The 100x Developer

- Most code is no longer read line by line by a human
- Routine checks happen without asking for approval
- Agents review, test, commit, and deploy
- Humans watch outcomes, risk, and exceptions
- Failures arrive with evidence—not a mystery
- The job becomes improving the system

## The Big Shift

<div class="ownership-shift">
  <div class="side before"><strong class="highlight-orange">10x: inspect the work</strong><br><br>Read the diff<br>Check each step<br>Approve the move</div>
  <div class="middle">→</div>
  <div class="side after"><strong style="color:#ff7b72">100x: inspect the outcome</strong><br><br>Watch the result<br>Review exceptions<br>Improve the rules</div>
</div>

<p class="big-idea">Less reading. Less routine checking.<br><span class="accent">More attention where it matters.</span></p>

## Less Checking ≠ Less Safety

<div class="card-grid four">
  <div class="idea-card orange"><strong>Tests</strong>Run automatically</div>
  <div class="idea-card orange"><strong>Limits</strong>Stop risky changes</div>
  <div class="idea-card red"><strong>Review</strong>Agents challenge agents</div>
  <div class="idea-card red"><strong>Escalation</strong>Humans see exceptions</div>
</div>

<p class="big-idea">Human checking falls.<br><span class="accent-orange">Total checking rises.</span></p>

## Autonomy Is Earned

<div class="trust-ladder">
  <div class="trust-step">Suggest</div>
  <div class="trust-step">Draft</div>
  <div class="trust-step">Act, then ask</div>
  <div class="trust-step">Act and report</div>
  <div class="trust-step">Handle exceptions</div>
</div>

<p class="plain-note">Do not jump to the top. Promote workflows that keep proving themselves.</p>

## The 10x developer

- AI participates across the whole delivery loop
- You specify outcomes and acceptance criteria before code
- Agents work on small vertical slices
- You review behavior and evidence, not just diffs
- Every correction becomes a test, tool, or instruction
- Verification is now the bottleneck

## The 100x developer

- You manage a delivery system, not an editor
- Kanban becomes an executable queue
- Agents code, review, commit, and deploy
- Humans own intent, taste, risk, and exceptions
- The system is observable, reversible, and self-checking
- Your job is improving the loop
